topics.title: B. Sunnyslope Housing — Restricted-Use Property Worth Less Than Foreclosure
topics.description: Ninth Circuit en banc casebook note (not full opinion): lower retained-use value than foreclosure.

entries.title: Sunnyslope restricted affordability use creates valuation inversion
entries.source: Uploaded Bankruptcy casebook Chapter 6 §B: Sunnyslope Housing note, full Till v. SCS Credit Corp. plurality, concurrence and dissent; original textbook discussion on present value
entries.summary: In re Sunnyslope Housing (9th Cir en banc 2017) involved affordable housing project restricted to low-income rents under continued use; foreclosure extinguished restrictions. Lender $9m claim; proposed continued-use value $3.9m, foreclosure unencumbered value $7m.
entries.laymanExplanation: Foreclosure unlocks high rents, but debtor proposes continuing affordable rents; keeping property might be worth LESS.
entries.legalExplanation: Ninth Circuit 8–3 en banc majority applied Rash actual proposed use and chose $3.9m; dissent wanted $7m foreclosure floor based on lender protection/double risks.
entries.examApplication: Compare actual proposed collateral use and whether lienholder should have foreclosure floor when higher.
entries.examTrap: This is a casebook explanatory note, not full court opinion provided.

entries.title: Dissent viewed Rash double risks as possible foreclosure-value minimum
entries.source: Uploaded Bankruptcy casebook Chapter 6 §B: Sunnyslope Housing note, full Till v. SCS Credit Corp. plurality, concurrence and dissent; original textbook discussion on present value
entries.summary: Minority argued §506(a)'s creditor-interest focus and Rash risk discussion suggest foreclosure value as minimum where use value is much lower.
entries.laymanExplanation: Lender argues cannot be forced to take $3.9m when seizure yields $7m.
entries.legalExplanation: Casebook explicitly raises whether double-risk rationale was dicta and how Till Thomas references it.
entries.examApplication: In exam show competing statutory interpretation and practical creditor fairness.
entries.examTrap: Do not convert dissent floor into Ninth Circuit majority holding.

entries.title: Two numbers, one actual proposed plan
entries.source: Uploaded Bankruptcy casebook Chapter 6 §B: Sunnyslope Housing note, full Till v. SCS Credit Corp. plurality, concurrence and dissent; original textbook discussion on present value
entries.summary: If creditor claim is $9m, foreclosure $7m, retained affordable housing use $3.9m, analyze §506(a) secured amount by retained use even though difference unusual.
entries.laymanExplanation: What debtor actually does with property matters more than theoretical most profitable use under Rash.
entries.legalExplanation: The Ninth Circuit en banc use valuation is grounded to lawful restrictive covenants that persist absent foreclosure.
entries.examApplication: Use this to test whether you understand Rash isn't invariably creditor-high valuation.
entries.examTrap: Do not blindly select higher number for secured creditor every time.

topics.title: B. Cramdown Payments: Present Value, Discount Rate, Loan Formula
topics.description: The separate problem of amount of collateral-backed claim and time value of deferred installments.

entries.title: Valuing collateral is separate from discounting future plan installments
entries.source: Uploaded Bankruptcy casebook Chapter 6 §B: Sunnyslope Housing note, full Till v. SCS Credit Corp. plurality, concurrence and dissent; original textbook discussion on present value
entries.summary: §506(a) determines allowed secured PRINCIPAL. §§1325(a)(5)(B)(ii), 1225(a)(5)(B)(ii), 1129(b)(2)(A)(i)(II) require future payment stream whose value at plan effective date at least that principal.
entries.laymanExplanation: First decide debt backed by car; then calculate interest necessary if paid over time.
entries.legalExplanation: Rash addressed first question; Till addresses interest/discount in second.
entries.examApplication: Label calculations 'collateral valuation' and 'present value payment' separately.
entries.examTrap: A $4k secured claim paid $4k in future installments with zero interest generally has lower present value.

entries.title: Present-value discounting formula
entries.source: Uploaded Bankruptcy casebook Chapter 6 §B: Sunnyslope Housing note, full Till v. SCS Credit Corp. plurality, concurrence and dissent; original textbook discussion on present value
entries.summary: For cash installments CF_t at future periods t, present value PV = Σ[CF_t/(1+r)^t] for matching periodic discount rate r. If PV must equal allowed secured claim S, choose payment stream satisfying PV≥S.
entries.laymanExplanation: A dollar next year isn't worth a dollar today; discount each future payment then add.
entries.legalExplanation: Time value from opportunity cost/inflation; Till plurality also includes debtor default risk in chosen annual prime-plus discount rate.
entries.examApplication: If all payments annual, divide by (1+r) to year t; if monthly, convert rate/frequency consistently.
entries.examTrap: Don't simply add nominal installments and compare sum to principal.

entries.title: Level installment payment formula
entries.source: Uploaded Bankruptcy casebook Chapter 6 §B: Sunnyslope Housing note, full Till v. SCS Credit Corp. plurality, concurrence and dissent; original textbook discussion on present value
entries.summary: If S present value secured claim, n equal end-of-period installments and periodic r>0, payment A = S·r/[1−(1+r)^(-n)]. For r=0, A=S/n. This is a mathematical study aid, not original problem answer.
entries.laymanExplanation: Calculator for identical monthly car payments over n months.
entries.legalExplanation: Choose r per month if n months (e.g., annual rate /12 when nominal monthly convention appropriate). Fees/compounding may change legal actual amount.
entries.examApplication: Sample independent: $10,000 secured over 12 monthly payments at nominal 12% annual, r=.01; use formula rather than $10k/12.
entries.examTrap: Don't confuse simple interest on full principal with amortization declining balance.

entries.title: Formula interest: national prime plus evidence-based risk adjustment
entries.source: Uploaded Bankruptcy casebook Chapter 6 §B: Sunnyslope Housing note, full Till v. SCS Credit Corp. plurality, concurrence and dissent; original textbook discussion on present value
entries.summary: Till Stevens four-Justice plurality favors national prime rate plus appropriate percentage reflecting plan risk, estate circumstances, collateral, duration and feasibility; in case prime 8% + risk 1.5%=9.5%.
entries.laymanExplanation: Start from benchmark for healthy loans, then add extra risk for bankruptcy borrower.
entries.legalExplanation: As source describes, courts usually considered 1–3% adjustments but no universal required increment set by Till; plan not confirmed if overly risky.
entries.examApplication: Distinguish source-case factual 8/1.5/9.5 from present-day prime (not supplied).
entries.examTrap: Never plug today's prime or generic 1.5% into source hypothetical without facts.

entries.title: Competing discount-rate approaches
entries.source: Uploaded Bankruptcy casebook Chapter 6 §B: Sunnyslope Housing note, full Till v. SCS Credit Corp. plurality, concurrence and dissent; original textbook discussion on present value
entries.summary: Four approaches debated: national prime-plus formula, hypothetical coerced/forced loan market comparable, presumptive original contract rate, and lender cost of borrowing; Till plurality rejected last three for Chapter13.
entries.laymanExplanation: Different people ask whose market you value: borrower's new loan, old contract, lender financing, or benchmark plus risk.
entries.legalExplanation: Scalia dissent preferred rebuttable contract rate, Thomas concurrence risk-free; holding/judgment 5–4 but reasoning no majority.
entries.examApplication: On exam write 4 approaches and each rationale, note lack majority.
entries.examTrap: Do not call Stevens's plurality a 5-Justice majority.

entries.title: Risk premium and feasibility must be balanced
entries.source: Uploaded Bankruptcy casebook Chapter 6 §B: Sunnyslope Housing note, full Till v. SCS Credit Corp. plurality, concurrence and dissent; original textbook discussion on present value
entries.summary: Plurality said rate high enough to compensate creditor for nonpayment risk but not arbitrarily minimized to make unworkable plan appear feasible; §1325(a)(6) mandates feasible plan.
entries.laymanExplanation: If only sky-high interest covers risk, judge may need to reject plan.
entries.legalExplanation: Default probability, collateral depreciation, liquidation and enforcement costs can inform risk adjustment; creditor bears evidence burden under plurality approach.
entries.examApplication: For interest dispute compare risk input to proof and feasibility facts.
entries.examTrap: Plan feasibility doesn't mathematically guarantee creditor zero default risk.

entries.title: Interest rate not identical to historical contract rate
entries.source: Uploaded Bankruptcy casebook Chapter 6 §B: Sunnyslope Housing note, full Till v. SCS Credit Corp. plurality, concurrence and dissent; original textbook discussion on present value
entries.summary: Under plurality, cramdown is imposed supervised debt treatment, not refinancing by original lender on identical commercial terms; 21% subprime contract includes factors such as profit/transaction costs.
entries.laymanExplanation: Old 21% contract interest isn't automatically what creditor gets on forced Chapter13 plan.
entries.legalExplanation: Cramdown changes right to price; objective secured claim value rather than lender's opportunity to make outside loan.
entries.examApplication: When creditor argues 21% compare prime-plus and market-risk concerns.
entries.examTrap: Don't claim 21% is necessarily too high in all cases, dispute is factual/legal.

topics.title: B. Till v. SCS Credit Corp. (2004) — Full Plurality, Concurrence and Dissent
topics.description: Detailed appellate and Supreme Court rationales for Chapter13 discount rate.

entries.title: Till v. SCS Credit Corp., 541 U.S. 465 (2004)
entries.source: Uploaded Bankruptcy casebook Chapter 6 §B: Sunnyslope Housing note, full Till v. SCS Credit Corp. plurality, concurrence and dissent; original textbook discussion on present value
entries.summary: Supreme Court reversed Seventh Circuit 5–4 but no single majority rationale. Stevens plurality (4 Justices) favored prime-plus objective formula to account for time and plan default risk and approved 9.5% on case record. Thomas concurred in judgment but would not require debtor-specific risk premium; Scalia four-Justice dissent favored rebuttable prebankruptcy contract rate 21% as better risk proxy.
entries.laymanExplanation: Chapter13 cramdown requires present value of allowed secured claim. Stevens plurality's prime-plus approach is influential, but no majority endorsed a particular rate-setting methodology; Thomas concurred only in judgment and dissents rejected formula.
entries.legalExplanation: Stevens rejected coerced-loan market and original contract as creditor-focused, costly, possibly profits/transaction-cost inflated; lender's cost of funds measures wrong party. Prime baseline plus case-specific risk adjustment familiar/objective, evidence primarily creditor supplied; feasibility §1325(a)(6) avoids unworkable plans. Thomas parsed statutory 'property to be distributed' rather than value of risky promise, thus a risk-free rate could suffice; because 9.5% higher, he agreed. Scalia thought subprime markets and contract rate better reflect failure, collateral depreciation, liquidity, enforcement risk; prime+1.5% may severely undercompensate lenders. Stevens replied bankruptcy supervision changes risk and creditor has information advantage.
entries.examApplication: Use case figures 8% prime +1.5%=9.5% vs 21% original, $4k secured/$894.89 unsecured; explain why no majority on formula.
entries.examTrap: Do not present risk-free standard as holding or say 'Till unanimously requires prime+1–3%'.
entries.sourceRole: Full Supreme Court opinions excerpted from Chapter 6 (no single majority opinion)
entries.facts: Lee and Amy Till bought used truck Oct.2 1998 from Instant Auto Finance, purchase financed at 21% annual over 136 weeks, assigned to SCS. Filed joint Chapter13 Oct.25 1999 in default. $4,894.89 outstanding secured by truck worth stipulated $4k → $894.89 unsecured. Plan devoted $740/month wages over 3 years and paid secured part with 9.5% interest, derived 8% then-current prime +1.5 risk. SCS wanted 21% contract/subprime rate. Bankruptcy court confirmed 9.5%; district and Seventh Circuit reversed adopting creditor lending/contract baseline; Supreme Court reversed.
entries.issue: How to set interest/discount rate so deferred Chapter13 cramdown payments have present value at least secured claim under §1325(a)(5)(B)(ii)?
entries.holding: Supreme Court reversed Seventh Circuit 5–4 but no single majority rationale. Stevens plurality (4 Justices) favored prime-plus objective formula to account for time and plan default risk and approved 9.5% on case record. Thomas concurred in judgment but would not require debtor-specific risk premium; Scalia four-Justice dissent favored rebuttable prebankruptcy contract rate 21% as better risk proxy.
entries.reasoning: Stevens rejected coerced-loan market and original contract as creditor-focused, costly, possibly profits/transaction-cost inflated; lender's cost of funds measures wrong party. Prime baseline plus case-specific risk adjustment familiar/objective, evidence primarily creditor supplied; feasibility §1325(a)(6) avoids unworkable plans. Thomas parsed statutory 'property to be distributed' rather than value of risky promise, thus a risk-free rate could suffice; because 9.5% higher, he agreed. Scalia thought subprime markets and contract rate better reflect failure, collateral depreciation, liquidity, enforcement risk; prime+1.5% may severely undercompensate lenders. Stevens replied bankruptcy supervision changes risk and creditor has information advantage.
entries.rule: Chapter13 cramdown requires present value of allowed secured claim. Stevens plurality's prime-plus approach is influential, but no majority endorsed a particular rate-setting methodology; Thomas concurred only in judgment and dissents rejected formula.
entries.concurrence: Justice Thomas (one vote): §1325(a)(5)(B)(ii) requires value of PROPERTY to be distributed, not valuation of promise as risk-adjusted credit; risk-free present-value compensation enough under literal reading; 9.5% exceeds that. He connected Rash replacement value to protection against lender's risk of retaining collateral.
entries.dissent: Justice Scalia, joined by Chief Justice Rehnquist and Justices O'Connor and Kennedy (4 votes): presumptive contract 21% with opportunity to rebut best captures expected default risk, unlike prime-plus where guesswork risk premium likely too low; keys are plan failure probability, collateral depreciation, collateral market liquidity, enforcement costs. Bankruptcy supervision doesn't remove real plan failures.

entries.title: Plurality was FOUR justices; Thomas supplied fifth judgment vote
entries.source: Uploaded Bankruptcy casebook Chapter 6 §B: Sunnyslope Housing note, full Till v. SCS Credit Corp. plurality, concurrence and dissent; original textbook discussion on present value
entries.summary: Stevens/Souter/Ginsburg/Breyer plurality adopted formula; Thomas concurred only in judgment with risk-free rationale; Scalia/Rehnquist/O'Connor/Kennedy dissent preferred presumptive contract rate.
entries.laymanExplanation: Five justices agreed lower decision wrong, but not on precise best formula.
entries.legalExplanation: On exam identify fragmentation and use fact-reasoning approach rather than misstate holding.
entries.examTrap: 'Supreme Court held prime-plus is the only constitutional rate' is false.

entries.title: Case-specific 9.5% and 21% debate
entries.source: Uploaded Bankruptcy casebook Chapter 6 §B: Sunnyslope Housing note, full Till v. SCS Credit Corp. plurality, concurrence and dissent; original textbook discussion on present value
entries.summary: Prime about 8% plus risk adjustment 1.5% =9.5% proposed; SCS argued 21% based on original subprime contract and lender testimony; principal secured $4,000.
entries.laymanExplanation: They fought over interest applied to $4k secured debt, not total $4,894.89 owed.
entries.legalExplanation: Unsecured deficiency receives separate treatment; future installments present value test.
entries.examApplication: For question ask whom high rate benefits and whether deal remains feasible.
entries.examTrap: Don't apply interest to $894.89 unsecured amount as if fully secured.

entries.title: Plurality rejects coerced-loan, contract and cost-of-funds
entries.source: Uploaded Bankruptcy casebook Chapter 6 §B: Sunnyslope Housing note, full Till v. SCS Credit Corp. plurality, concurrence and dissent; original textbook discussion on present value
entries.summary: Hypothetical new loan rates import commercial profit/transaction costs, prior contract focuses subjective history, lender cost of funds depends on lender rather than debtor; costly hearings. Formula prime+increment is objective starting point.
entries.laymanExplanation: What bank normally charges isn't necessarily right for court-imposed plan payments.
entries.legalExplanation: Stevens analogized secured lender as entitled to objective time/risk compensation, not every alternative investment opportunity.
entries.examApplication: Discuss both administrative simplicity and economic objections.
entries.examTrap: Market lending evidence may still inform risk disputes in other circumstances.

entries.title: Thomas concurrence: a promise is risky, but property may not be
entries.source: Uploaded Bankruptcy casebook Chapter 6 §B: Sunnyslope Housing note, full Till v. SCS Credit Corp. plurality, concurrence and dissent; original textbook discussion on present value
entries.summary: Thomas read §1325(a)(5)(B)(ii) as discounting 'property to be distributed' not risky promissory obligation; time value yes but debtor-specific nonpayment risk not necessarily part of statutory PV requirement.
entries.laymanExplanation: He says court shouldn't build debtor credit score risk into the value of cash itself.
entries.legalExplanation: He treated Rash replacement valuation of collateral as already protecting lender partly against retention risks.
entries.examApplication: Compare Thomas to Stevens/Scalia on two fundamental financial principles: time and risk.
entries.examTrap: His reading did not get majority.

entries.title: Scalia dissent: rebuttable contract-rate approach
entries.source: Uploaded Bankruptcy casebook Chapter 6 §B: Sunnyslope Housing note, full Till v. SCS Credit Corp. plurality, concurrence and dissent; original textbook discussion on present value
entries.summary: Start with parties' 21% contract rate as approximate actual subprime risk; parties may show current markets or contract idiosyncrasy call for change. Prime baseline is knowingly too low and risk add-on hard to estimate.
entries.laymanExplanation: Old loan documents may contain better market risk pricing than judge's guess at +1.5%.
entries.legalExplanation: Scalia highlighted plan failure, depreciation, collateral liquidity and costly enforcement, and argued judicial confirmation isn't oracle.
entries.examApplication: Answer by comparison of burden and default statistics/market competitiveness, not by assuming Scalia was holding.
entries.examTrap: Do not automatically treat contract rate as binding; dissent would make it rebuttable.

entries.title: Why §1325(a)(6) feasibility does not settle rate alone
entries.source: Uploaded Bankruptcy casebook Chapter 6 §B: Sunnyslope Housing note, full Till v. SCS Credit Corp. plurality, concurrence and dissent; original textbook discussion on present value
entries.summary: Stevens believed court should deny plans if high risk requires eye-popping compensation and threatens viability. Scalia countered real-world failure rates undermine premise that confirmed plans are low risk.
entries.laymanExplanation: A plan declared feasible can still fail, but rate can't be set only to help plan pass.
entries.legalExplanation: Casebook questions juxtapose court administration/policy with creditor full compensation.
entries.examApplication: Mention feasibility is additional requirement, not alternative to present-value rate.
entries.examTrap: Not valid to choose zero discount just because trustee oversees payments.
